concept.title: Does classifying services help people find them?
concept.shortdesc: The same needs, answered by searching the text of each service and by using the three classifications (service type, audience, eligibility), compared.

conbody.note: Every judgement here was made by a language model, and no person has re-judged any of them. Read the numbers as a first measurement of a draft, not as a result.
conbody.p: asked whether a person can find a suitable service. This page asks a narrower question: does it help to index every service by the three classifications, compared with searching the text of its description? Every service in every directory that could be read was given a service-type, an audience and an eligibility category (a service that sits between two categories also carries a second label). For each need, in each place, each route below produced a list of five services, and the services were judged blind as suitable, unusable for this person (wrong eligibility) or not suitable. There were 165 need-and-place cases; the figures below use the 154 where the judges found a suitable service by some route.

ul.li: Search put a suitable service in the top five for 94% of cases. The best route that uses the classifications, service type, audience, eligibility, topped up, did so for 90%. That is not clearly better than search: the difference is -0.04 [-0.12, +0.02].
On this measure the idea that classifying services finds them better than searching their text is not supported. No route that uses the classifications beat search on the hit rate.

The classifications do reduce a different failure: a service of the right kind that the person cannot use (for example one that needs a referral they do not have). Search put such a service in 18% of its results; the routes that use audience and eligibility did so in 11% to 14%.

Using the classifications first and filling the list from search, with the age filter, gives the fewest unusable services in this run: it finds a suitable service for 89% of cases (search 94%) with 11% of the five unusable (search 18%).

Second labels add services of about the same quality as those found by a first label, but they change the top five in few cases, because a linked category usually already holds five or more services. They help most where a category is small.

The age filter removes services whose stated age range excludes the person. It reduces the services the person could not use and does not clearly change the hit rate. It can only act where a service states an age, which most directories do for few services.

section.p: For the needs the catalogue marks as safety needs, a missed result matters most. Few cases, so treat the figures as an indication.

section.title: How to read it, and what is not yet known

ul.li: The judges saw only the person's need and each service's own description, in a batch that did not say which route had chosen it.

Hit rate is the share of cases where a suitable service was in the top five. Services are judged only when some route returned them, so the number of suitable services is a lower bound and recall is understated for every route.

The age bands for each need were written by the person running the study from the need's description. A person has not reviewed them. The band for a parent-and-baby need includes the parent's age, which was added after a first look at the results.
Three needs have no linked service-type category, so the routes that depend on one return nothing for them.
Only services whose descriptions could be restated are in any route; the rest of each directory is not.
One judge, one pass. In an earlier run of this comparison every service was judged a second time, and 153 of 165 (93%) kept the same label. The services added later were judged once.
Nothing here is a pass mark. The pass marks for the draft are still placeholders.
